blocks.text:
Can a Markdown artifact carry enough admitted history for a receiver with no
shared conversation or Git ledger to recover what changed, why, and which
consequential direction was rejected?

The sender created a portable v1, accepted a v2 with an explicit reason and one
consequential rejection, and copied the original Markdown file into a fresh Git
repository. The receiver had no sender ledger ref or session history. It ran
`inspect`, `import`, and `log` against the renamed file.

A separate set of cases introduced an IDE-style body edit, corrupted the
capsule, switched through a private local interval, produced a clean copy,
renamed the artifact, invoked fallback capture, and attempted a snapshot from a
stale base.

- The receiver restored the same path-independent artifact identity.
- The accepted v2 reason and consequential rejection survived the handoff.
- Casual discussion was absent because no caller admitted it.
- An unrecorded body edit failed both `inspect` and `verify`.
- Capsule corruption failed inspection.
- Re-enabling portable after a local interval exposed no private interval data.
- A clean export contained no transport metadata and did not mutate the source.
- Fallback capture attributed only the recorder, not an editor or producer.
- A stale base was rejected before it could become the next version.
- Leading YAML frontmatter remained at byte zero.

The executable suite contains ten passing black-box cases covering these
behaviors.

This validates a byte-preserving file handoff across isolated repositories. It
does not prove that every Slack, email, wiki, formatter, or copy/paste path
preserves the hidden carrier. If a transport strips metadata, the result is an
ordinary readable Markdown artifact with no provenance claim. A real Slack
attachment round-trip remains a release-channel check.

It also does not prove authorship cryptographically. Body, chain, semantic diff,
and claims are checkable; `why` and actor fields remain attributed testimony.

> Proofpress makes a Markdown artifact carry a checkable record of its admitted
> changes and attributed decision context—even when it leaves Git.

Avoid “complete history,” “verified why,” “confidential hidden metadata,” and
“works through every sharing channel.”
